name: Saloon 4350
summary: Two-floor dining pub near Gyodae with a huge sound system, draught Guinness, whisky highballs and hearty plates.
description: Saloon 4350 bills itself as a luxury dining pub with an 'overwhelming' speaker system, and music is part of the draw: Naver reviewers single out the sound (185 mentions). It spreads over two floors on Seocho-daero 46-gil, 3 min from Gyodae, so a group of 5 can sprawl. The menu covers draught Guinness and Stella, craft pale ale, highballs from Kakubin to Hakushu, bottles of wine and single malts. The food is substantial: Chicago-style pizza, a sirloin steak with ghee butter, gambas and golbaengi.

summary: Underground Hannam bar inspired by 1920s East-meets-West drinking culture; No. 89 in Asia's 50 Best Bars 2026.
description: Soko is a basement bar in Hannam-dong, led by bartender-owner Son Soko and inspired by 1920s drinking culture where East and West met. It pairs a buzzing, clubby energy with precise classics, and serves hearty food such as fried chicken and steak. It has appeared on Asia's 50 Best Bars lists every year since 2023, at No. 89 in 2026. It is less known to tourists than the Cheongdam speakeasies.

name: Southside Parlor

summary: Itaewon favourite for fresh-juice craft cocktails, Texas BBQ and southern hospitality, with a 4th-floor rooftop.
description: Southside Parlor has been a Seoul cocktail institution for more than a decade, founded to bring craft cocktails, Texas BBQ and southern hospitality to Itaewon. Every juice is fresh-squeezed and every syrup house-made, and the kitchen turns out burgers, brisket, tacos and wings that make it a full dinner stop. English is the house language, so it is the most relaxed choice on this list for parents.

subcategory: Hotel whisky & cocktail bar with live music
summary: Park Hyatt's basement vinyl-and-whisky bar: Korean-accented cocktails, sushi plates and live jazz or soul sets most nights.
description: The Timber House is in the lower level of Park Hyatt Seoul, directly above Samseong Station. After a renovation it reopened as a vinyl music bar with wood, stone and brick rooms, walls of records, a grand piano and a small stage, split into several intimate seating areas. Drinks focus on premium whisky and signature cocktails that use Korean ingredients. The kitchen does Japanese izakaya plates, sashimi and a sushi omakase. The venue's Naver notice lists live sets every night from 20:30 through September 2026. There is no view here: it is a moody, windowless room, which makes it a good pick for a rainy night.
highlights: Live sets from 20:30 nightly (2 sets Mon–Tue, 3 sets later in the week, per the venue's September 2026 notice)

tips: Arrive at 17:00 for the half-price Groove Hour, eat, then stay for the 20:30 set. This is the value play in an expensive hotel bar.
DiningCode reviewers report a music charge of about ₩10,000 per person during evening performances. Confirm when booking (+82-2-2016-1235).
For 5 people, reserve a table rather than the counter. Naver marks the venue as a no-kids zone, which is not an issue for an adult group.
Take Samseong Station (Line 2) Exit 1; the hotel entrance is right at the exit. Per Naver, valet parking is free and self-parking costs ₩10,000 for the first 3 hours.

name: Zest
summary: Zero-waste cocktail bar ranked No. 2 in Asia's 50 Best Bars 2026 and Korea's best bar four years running.
description: Zest is the most decorated bar in Korea: No. 2 on Asia's 50 Best Bars for a third straight year and named Best Bar in Korea for the fourth time in 2026. The team works to a zero-waste philosophy, making sodas and spirits in-house and turning leftover peel and pulp into new ingredients. Their gin uses Korean botanicals, and drinks such as the Jeju Garibaldi (hallabong juice with house citrus-peel gin) show off local produce. The ground-floor room on Dosan-daero 55-gil near Apgujeong Rodeo is bright, calm and table-served, so it works better for a group than a counter-only speakeasy.
highlights: Jeju Garibaldi with hallabong juice and house gin
tips: Book a few days ahead for a table of 5; weekend evenings fill first. Walk-ins have the best odds at the 18:30 opening.
Opens at 15:00 on Sat and Sun, so an afternoon drink is an easy way to get a table without booking.
TripAdvisor reviewers mention cocktails at around ₩25,000 each. Valet parking is available.

description: Banpo Bridge’s 1,140 m fountain sprays in time to music, lit in rainbow colours after dark, and is watched from the lawns and steps of Banpo Hangang Park. name: Bukchon Hanok Village
summary: Hillside lanes of tiled-roof hanok homes between two palaces — a lived-in residential area with visiting hours.
description: Bukchon is the largest cluster of traditional hanok houses in Seoul, climbing the slope between Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung. The famous alleys of Bukchon-ro 11-gil frame hanok roofs against downtown towers. People still live here: since 2025 the core zone is a special management area with tourist visiting hours (about 10:00–17:00) and fines for entering outside them.
tips: Respect the visiting-hour rules in the red zone (roughly 10:00–17:00) and keep voices low — it is a residential area.
Steep slopes: for parents, start at the top (taxi to Samcheong-dong) and walk downhill.
Combine with Gyeongbokgung (free during Chuseok) and the Samcheong-dong cafés.

name: Changdeokgung Palace & Secret Garden
summary: UNESCO palace that follows the hills, with Huwon, the Joseon kings’ Secret Garden, on a guided tour.
description: Changdeokgung was the Joseon kings’ favourite residence and is the palace most in harmony with its landscape, which earned it UNESCO status. The main grounds are free during Chuseok, but the Secret Garden (Huwon) — ponds, pavilions and a centuries-old juniper — is seen only on a timed, paid tour. The garden route is hilly and takes about 90 minutes.
highlights: Buyongji pond and Juhamnu pavilion in the Secret Garden
Autumn colour in the Huwon woods
tips: The Secret Garden is EXCLUDED from free Chuseok entry — book the tour online ahead; slots sell out on holidays.
Closed Mondays — 28 Sep is closed.
The garden walk climbs; parents who dislike stairs can enjoy the flat main palace and skip Huwon.
Walk straight on into Changgyeonggung next door via the connecting gate.

name: Cheonggyecheon Stream
summary: A restored stream running below street level through downtown — cool, quiet and softly lit at night.
description: Once buried under an elevated highway, Cheonggyecheon was reopened in 2005 as a 10 km walkway below the city. name: Deoksugung Palace
summary: Compact downtown palace mixing Joseon halls with a neoclassical stone hall, open until 21:00 and lit at night.
description: Deoksugung sits beside City Hall and is small enough to see in an hour, which makes it ideal for an evening stroll. name: Gyeongbokgung Palace
summary: Seoul’s grandest Joseon palace, backed by Bugaksan — and free during Chuseok 24–27 Sep 2026 with guard ceremonies.
description: Built in 1395, Gyeongbokgung is the largest of Seoul’s five royal palaces, with the throne hall Geunjeongjeon and the lotus-pond pavilion Gyeonghoeru set against the mountains. The courtyards are wide and flat, so the walking is easy for parents. The National Folk Museum sits inside the grounds. During Chuseok 2026 admission is free and the royal guard ceremonies run daily.

name: Heyri Art Valley and Paju Book City
summary: A village of architect-designed galleries and cafés north of Seoul, ten minutes from Paju Book City — pairs with the Paju outlet.
description: Heyri Art Valley is an artists' village built under design rules rather than a single style, so every building on the street is different, with galleries, artist studios, outdoor sculpture, cafés and bookshops free to walk between (individual galleries charge their own admission). Paju Book City, the Korean publishing industry's own architecture district, is ten minutes further on. The 2200 bus from Hapjeong is the simplest way there; several galleries close on Mondays, though the village itself does not. Pairs naturally with Lotte Premium Outlet Paju for a full day out.

name: Songdo Central Park
summary: A seawater canal through a city built from nothing in 20 years, best at dusk when the towers light up.
description: Songdo Central Park runs a 1.8 km seawater canal (with boats on it) through Incheon's planned international business district, built on reclaimed mud flats. The Tri-bowl — three inverted domes over a reflecting pool — sits at the eastern end, and a deer park and hanok village sit at the far end. It is flat and free to walk, and it is genuinely a different visit at dusk, once the surrounding towers light up, than in flat daylight. Incheon Line 1 runs directly to Central Park station.

tips: Arrive an hour before sunset — the park is ordinary in flat daylight and good once the towers switch on behind it.

name: Suwon Hwaseong
summary: A complete 18th-century city wall, 5.5 km of it, with a restored palace inside — the easiest day trip on the list by train.
description: Suwon Hwaseong is a complete UNESCO-listed fortress wall from 1796, 5.5 km around, with a town that still lives inside the gates and a restored royal palace, Hwaseong Haenggung, in the middle. Walking the full loop means a climb over Paldalsan; the flat northern stretch from Janganmun to Hwaseomun is the good part for a family that wants the view without the hill. The wall itself is free and open 24 hours; only the palace charges admission. Line 1 runs directly to Suwon Station from central Seoul, making this the simplest day trip out of the eight covered here, but budget most of a day including local transfer from the station to the wall — it is well outside the subway network the family uses at home.
highlights: 5.5 km UNESCO fortress wall, free and open 24 h
Hwaseong Haenggung palace inside the walls, ticketed
Flat northern stretch: Janganmun to Hwaseomun
A local tram service covers the fortress loop for anyone who does not want to walk it all
tips: Walk the Janganmun-to-Hwaseomun section, which is level, and skip the southern hill over Paldalsan.
The walls are free and open all the time; only the palace is ticketed.
Consider the Hwaseong tourist tram for the sections you'd rather not walk — it loops the fortress and saves the family's legs.

name: Namdaemun Market
summary: Korea’s oldest and biggest market: 10,000 stalls of kitchenware, ginseng, clothes, hotteok and kalguksu alley.
description: Namdaemun Market spreads around Sungnyemun Gate with more than 10,000 stores selling almost everything, from kitchenware, glasses and accessories to ginseng, seaweed and children’s clothing. description: Lotte World Aquarium fills the basement of Lotte World Mall in Jamsil with 13 themed zones modelled on the world’s oceans, an escalator-tunnel entrance, a large main ocean tank and walk-through tunnel, plus seals, otters and penguins. It is bright, modern and easy to combine with the mall and tower. TripAdvisor states that it does not currently meet its animal-welfare policy (earlier reviews raised concerns about beluga whales), so families who care about this may prefer SEA LIFE COEX.
tips: Combine with Lotte World Mall and Seoul Sky in one Jamsil day; Jamsil Station (Line 2/8).
Weekday mornings are calmer; buy tickets online to skip the counter.

name: Paradise City
summary: A resort on Yeongjong Island with a foreigners-only casino floor, a free public art space and an outdoor art plaza.
description: Paradise City is a joint venture between Paradise Group and Sega Sammy next to Incheon Airport. Its casino floor — Korea's largest gaming space open to foreign passport holders and overseas residents (Korean nationals are legally excluded, not just by house policy) — sits alongside a free Art Space gallery and Wonderbox, a separate "night carnival" indoor attraction with rides and lighting design aimed at a family or date-night crowd rather than the casino itself. It is a genuine day out of Seoul near the airport.
highlights: Foreigners-only casino floor, 8,726㎡ of gaming space
Wonderbox: indoor "night carnival" theme attraction with rides
Free Art Space gallery and outdoor Wave art plaza
tips: Korean nationals cannot enter the casino floor; check who is in the party before planning around it.

name: Piknic
summary: A 1970s factory on the Namsan slope turned exhibition house, reopening 25 September with a show about the just-demolished Hilton Seoul.
description: Piknic is a converted small factory on the Namsan slope run by design studio Glint, known for shows that mix exhibition and atmosphere — Ryuichi Sakamoto's 2018 sound installation is the one people still mention. Between exhibitions the building closes entirely, and the new show, "Hilton Seoul, An Autobiography," opens 25 September 2026 — the trip lands in its opening week. The building itself is part of the show: exposed concrete, oddly shaped rooms, and a rooftop terrace looking back at Namsan, included with the ticket.

tips: Between shows the building closes entirely — do not go before 25 September.

name: Seoul Dal
summary: A tethered helium balloon lifting 30 people about 130 m over Yeouido Park on a winch — nothing about it is adrenal.
description: Seoul Dal is a cable-controlled, winch-operated balloon that lifts about 30 seated passengers roughly 130 metres over Yeouido Park for around 15 minutes. It opened August 2024 and passed 20,000 riders in its first hundred days. There is nothing to steer, nothing to pilot, and it runs until 23:00 on Fridays and Saturdays, when the river and bridges are lit rather than just visible.
highlights: Runs to 23:00 Fri/Sat for the lit night view
tips: Weather cancels it — check before travelling.
Go on a clear evening; it runs to 23:00 Fri/Sat and the bridges are better lit than the daytime view.

name: Smurf Magic Forest
summary: Walk-in Smurf village under Gangnam: glowing forest sets, story-based escape missions, café and shop — near home.
description: Smurf Magic Forest bills itself as an urban mini theme park in a Gangnam basement near Sinnonhyeon. summary: Banyan Tree's own spa, set in the Namsan woods: private suites with baths, Asian massage and an 80-minute head spa.
description: Banyan Tree Club & Spa Seoul is an urban resort on the forested east slope of Namsan, and its spa on the lobby floor (3F, The Club) is the brand's original Asian spa concept. Therapists trained at Banyan Tree's academy work by hand with herbal, natural products. Every full treatment includes 30 minutes of 'Calm Time' with a foot bath and tea. It is the splurge pick for parents who want a quiet, luxurious afternoon, and it pairs easily with a Namsan walk or dinner in Jangchung-dong.

name: Spa Lei (women only)
summary: Women-only 24h bathhouse by Sinsa Station: seawater and open-air baths, a pine-fired bulhanjeungmak and famous body scrubs.
description: Spa Lei is a women-only sauna and jjimjilbang in Jamwon-dong, a few minutes' walk from Sinsa Station and one stop from home on Line 3. The spa styles itself on Eastern European bathhouses, with dark wood, framed photographs and a small open-air bath on a terrace, alongside a West Coast seawater bath, green-tea bath and a cold plunge that regulars rave about. The traditional bulhanjeungmak (fire-heated dome sauna) is lit with Gangwon pine at 5 am and opens at 10 am; there are also red-clay, charcoal and salt rooms. Seshin (Korean body scrub), oil massage, facials and nails are sold in-house, which is what most foreign reviewers come for.

name: SPAREX Dongmyo
summary: A modern 24h jjimjilbang on the 13th floor above Dongmyo Station, with a fire-kiln sauna, hinoki bath and city views, for ₩14,000.
description: SPAREX Dongmyo is a newer branch of the SPAREX chain, opened around 2024 on the 13th floor of the building beside Dongmyo Station. It replaces the big old-school bathhouses that closed after COVID, including Dragon Hill Spa and Siloam Sauna. It is bright and modern, with gender-separated baths and dry and wet saunas, then a shared hall in spa clothes with a bulhanjeungmak (fire-heated dome), hwangto clay, salt, ice and hinoki rooms. There is also a food court serving sikhye, roasted eggs and Korean set meals, a well-equipped gym and screen golf. Locals love it: 7,700+ Naver reviews single out how clean it is, its size and its fair price.
highlights: Bulhanjeungmak fire domes and a hinoki forest-bath room
Food court: sikhye, roasted eggs, jeyuk and miyeok-guk
tips: Hidden gem: over 7,700 Naver visitor reviews but only a handful on TripAdvisor. Go straight out of Dongmyo Station Exit 6 and up to the 13th floor.
Entry is ₩14,000 from 05:00–20:00 or ₩16,000 from 20:00–05:00, valid for 24 hours. Parking is free for 3 hours (official Instagram, June 2026).
Bring your own shampoo and a few ₩1,000 notes or coins, because hairdryers are coin-operated. Baths close for cleaning late at night (women's roughly 23:00–01:00, men's 00:00–02:00).
Pair it with the Dongmyo flea market or Dongdaemun (one stop on Line 1 or 6). It is also a cheap, rainy-evening reset for a group of 5.

reviews.text: A September 2026 reviewer found everything clean because it is fairly new. They liked the high-floor views, the jeyuk and seaweed-soup dinner and the reasonable price, and plan to return.
Another reviewer found the scrub short and the food-court tteokbokki and ramyeon undercooked. They called the food the weak spot.
A traveller said their scrub was excellent and very thorough, and that they 'felt like a new woman'.
A first-timer said nobody explained how the spa worked. Know the routine (shoe locker, bath, spa clothes) before you go.

name: Sulwhasoo Flagship Store & Spa
summary: Sulwhasoo’s golden lantern-like flagship in Dosan: ginseng-luxury skincare floors with a spa for Korean herbal facials.
description: Amorepacific’s luxury herbal brand Sulwhasoo has a five-storey flagship near Dosan Park whose golden, lantern-inspired façade is a sight in itself. Inside are gold-netted ceilings, product floors and a spa with treatment rooms and bathing facilities where Sulwhasoo’s ginseng-based skincare is used in facials and body treatments. It suits parents who want a refined, quiet K-beauty experience rather than a busy drugstore.

Full Sulwhasoo range across several floors

name: Supsok Hanbang Land
summary: A charcoal-kiln bathhouse on a wooded hill above Sinchon, where you roast sweet potatoes on the embers and rest on forest decks.
description: Supsok Hanbang Land (the 'forest herbal land') is one of the few Seoul jjimjilbangs that still fires real charcoal kilns (sutgama). There are low, medium and high-heat chambers, plus a hearth room where glowing charcoal sits in a brazier. It sits against Ansan's woods near Bongwonsa Temple, so between sweats you can cool off on shaded wooden decks outside. The snack bar sells sikhye and roasted eggs, and you can grill sweet potatoes, potatoes and rice cakes yourself; a separate restaurant grills samgyeopsal. Korean TV has featured it many times, and it is the most characterful of the classic big bathhouses left after Dragon Hill Spa and Siloam closed.
highlights: Charcoal kilns in three heat levels
Grill your own sweet potatoes and garaetteok (rice cakes)
tips: Bring socks, or buy them for ₩3,000: you need socks and a towel underfoot in the hottest kiln.
Adult bath plus sauna was ₩17,000 in July 2026, per a Naver review. Hairdryers are coin-operated and the coin noraebang takes cash only.
It is uphill from Sinchon and Ewha, so take a taxi from Ewha Womans Univ. Station on Line 2, direct from Seocho, rather than walking the slope with parents.
Weekends get crowded and noisy with kids. Arrive early on a weekday; the kilns run 08:00–21:00.

tripadvisor.rank: #107 of 512 Spas & Wellness in Seoul

reviews.text: A visitor called it another fantastic jjimjilbang, and even better after hiking nearby Ansan.
A reviewer loved roasting sweet potatoes and rice cakes, the variety of sauna rooms and the resident cat, and called it a one-of-a-kind jjimjilbang in Seoul.
Other recent reviews say the building and ice room are dated and service can be curt. Come for the kilns, not polish.

price.note: About ₩17,000 for bath plus charcoal kiln, or about ₩11,000 for bath only (Trip.com guide and a July 2026 Naver review). Snacks and grilling are extra.

summary: Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Deoksugung, Changgyeonggung and Jongmyo are free 24–27 Sep 2026, with guard ceremonies.
description: For Chuseok 2026 the Cultural Heritage Administration opens the four main palaces, Jongmyo and the Joseon royal tombs free of charge from 24 to 27 September. description: MMCA opens its Seoul, Gwacheon, Deoksugung and Cheongju branches free of charge for Chuseok.
